exonerate

ig-ZAH-nuh-rayt -- from Latin exonerare ('to unburden'), from ex- ('out, away') + onus/oneris ('a burden, load'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To exonerate is to officially clear someone of blame or wrongdoing, often after a formal review or new evidence.

A newly surfaced surveillance tape ultimately exonerated the shop owner, who had spent months under suspicion of insurance fraud.

Worked Example

The company's internal review found no evidence of wrongdoing and formally exonerated the manager, though her reputation took months to recover.

That official clearing of someone's name -- based on an investigation or new evidence rather than a courtroom verdict alone -- is exactly what it means to exonerate someone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pardon: A pardon officially forgives someone for an offense they are still considered to have committed — a governor may pardon a prisoner out of mercy. To exonerate points the other way: it clears a person of blame entirely, declaring the wrongdoing was never theirs.

forgive: To forgive is personal and emotional: the wronged person lets go of anger, and it happens in someone's heart, not on any record. To exonerate is public and official — a review or new evidence formally clears the person's name of blame.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

implicate: to show that someone is connected to a wrongdoing

convict: to formally declare someone guilty of a crime

Where it sits · how officially the blame is lifted — absolve → exonerate → acquit

absolve vs. exonerate: Absolve is milder than exonerate: a committee report can absolve volunteers of responsibility, while to exonerate someone is a stronger act — officially wiping away blame after formal review or new evidence.

acquit vs. exonerate: Acquit goes further than exonerate: a report may exonerate you from blame, but only an acquittal carries the heavier, binding force of a court verdict that ends the case for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-

prefix — ex-: out, away (Latin)

root — oner-

root — oner-: burden, load (Latin (onus/oneris))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ex- ('away') plus onus ('a burden') plus the verb suffix -ate. To exonerate someone is literally to lift the burden of blame off of them.

Use the root in a new word: onerous

Use the root in a new word: onerous: You may remember onerous from earlier in this course -- it describes a task so burdensome it feels like a heavy weight, the very burden exonerate removes.

Root Check

Word Choice

Exonerate is broader than acquit, taught earlier in this unit -- acquit specifically means a not-guilty court verdict, while exonerate can clear someone's name through an investigation, new evidence, or a resignation, with or without ever going to trial.
